issues.legal_issue: Off-duty conduct involving an alleged heinous crime may constitute disciplinary misconduct when it bears on a police employee’s fitness and public confidence in the police force.
material_facts: The employee was a police constable and was alleged to have been connected with a murder while on leave.
The disciplinary record included evidence of prior hostility and a death threat, and placed the employee and his tractor near the scene around the time the deceased was found.
The State’s case was that the employee’s connection with the incident undermined confidence in the police force.
issues.conclusion: The alleged conduct had a sufficient connection to the employee’s police service to be considered in disciplinary proceedings; the fact that it occurred outside duty did not prevent disciplinary action.
issues.legal_principle: A police employer may discipline an officer for conduct that breaches the standard expected of a member of the force and affects confidence in the police or the officer’s ability to serve. Rule 16 of the Rajasthan Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules 1958 governed the enquiry. The Court treated the nature of police employment and the public-administration implications of the alleged conduct as central.

rule.if: police_service_employee and off_duty_conduct_alleged and (heinous_conduct_connection or conduct_affects_public_confidence)

predicates.police_service_employee: The person concerned served as an employee of a police force.
predicates.off_duty_conduct_alleged: The employer alleged that the employee engaged in the conduct outside the performance of official duties.
predicates.heinous_conduct_connection: The employer relied on material connecting the employee to alleged serious criminal conduct.
predicates.conduct_affects_public_confidence: The employer relied on material indicating that the conduct could undermine public confidence in the police or the employee’s fitness to serve.

issues.definition: When a police employee is alleged to have engaged in off-duty conduct connected to serious wrongdoing or capable of undermining public confidence, that conduct may be considered in disciplinary proceedings.

issues.legal_issue: Misconduct in a disciplinary enquiry is assessed on the balance of probabilities, with the degree of probability depending on the subject matter, rather than by the criminal standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The disciplinary enquiry concerned allegations that the employee was involved in a murder and related service misconduct.
The disciplinary record included evidence of prior hostility and a threat, the employee’s presence near the scene, and the presence of his tractor nearby.
The criminal court acquitted the employee, but the disciplinary enquiry applied a different standard of proof.
issues.conclusion: The disciplinary enquiry was not required to establish the allegations beyond reasonable doubt; the relevant standard was a preponderance of probabilities, whose degree depends on the subject matter.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Suresh Pathrella v. Oriental Bank of Commerce and Samar Bahadur Singh v. State of U.P. for the distinction between criminal and disciplinary standards of proof. It relied on M. Siddiq v. Suresh Das, including its discussion of Miller v. Minister of Pensions and Bater v. Bater, for the principle that probabilities may have different degrees depending on the subject matter.

predicates.disciplinary_proceeding: An employer conducted a disciplinary enquiry into an employee’s alleged misconduct.
predicates.misconduct_alleged: The employer alleged conduct that could constitute a breach of the employee’s service obligations.

issues.definition: When an employer enquires into alleged employee misconduct, the allegation is assessed on whether it is more probable than not, with the required degree of probability informed by the subject matter.

issues.legal_issue: Judicial review of disciplinary findings is limited to checking for evidentiary support and legal perversity, and does not permit a court to reweigh evidence as an appellate fact-finder.
material_facts: The Division Bench examined the witness’s evidence, including cross-examination, and set aside the disciplinary outcome.
The disciplinary record also contained evidence beyond the witness’s cross-examination, including evidence of the employee’s proximity to the scene, prior hostility and a death threat.
The Division Bench’s reappraisal did not adequately address the broader evidentiary record and its bearing on the police force’s integrity and reputation.
issues.conclusion: The Division Bench’s criticism for reappraising the evidence as a first appellate court was justified, and its reasoning was deficient because it did not consider the broader evidentiary record. A reviewing court may intervene where findings are based on no evidence, are perverse, or fail to consider vital evidence, but may not substitute its own preferred view of the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Moni Shankar v. Union of India for the scope of judicial review and on P. John Chandy and Co. (P) Ltd. v. John P. Thomas for the need to consider a witness’s whole statement, including cross-examination. It also relied on State of U.P. v. Sheo Shanker Lal Srivastava and Coimbatore District Central Coop. Bank v. Employees Assn. concerning proportionality. Judicial review entails threshold scrutiny for some evidence and perversity, while respecting the disciplinary authority’s fact-finding role.

rule.if: disciplinary_finding_under_review and (reviewing_court_reweighs_evidence_as_appellate_court and finding_has_some_evidence and no_perversity)

predicates.disciplinary_finding_under_review: A court is reviewing a finding made in an employer’s disciplinary enquiry.
predicates.reviewing_court_reweighs_evidence_as_app: The reviewing court independently reassesses the evidence and substitutes its own view of the facts.
predicates.finding_has_some_evidence: The disciplinary finding has evidentiary material capable of supporting it.
predicates.no_perversity: The finding is not irrational or otherwise legally perverse.

issues.definition: When a disciplinary finding has evidentiary support and is not perverse, a reviewing court acts improperly if it reassesses the evidence as an appellate fact-finder and substitutes its own view.

issues.legal_issue: An acquittal in a criminal trial, including one based on benefit of doubt or witnesses turning hostile, does not by itself bar disciplinary proceedings or require reinstatement.
material_facts: The employee was acquitted of murder after the criminal court found the sole alleged eyewitness unreliable and several prosecution witnesses had turned hostile.
The disciplinary enquiry proceeded on a different evidentiary standard and addressed service-rule violations and the effect of the employee’s conduct on the police force.
The disciplinary authority relied on the criminal acquittal as an acquittal on benefit of doubt, not as a determination that eliminated the disciplinary case.
issues.conclusion: The criminal acquittal did not conclude the disciplinary enquiry or require reinstatement; the two proceedings could reach different outcomes because they apply different standards and address different matters.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Southern Railway Officers Association v. Union of India and Inspector General of Police v. S. Samuthiram. In discussing the expression “honourable acquittal,” it referred to RBI v. Bhopal Singh Panchal, R.P. Kapur v. Union of India, State of Assam v. Raghava Rajgopalachari and Robert Stuart Wauchope v. Emperor. It reiterated that criminal and disciplinary proceedings have different standards of proof and that the expression “honourable acquittal” is not found in the penal statutes or procedural code.

rule.if: disciplinary_proceeding and criminal_acquittal and (acquittal_based_on_benefit_of_doubt or prosecution_witnesses_turned_hostile)

predicates.disciplinary_proceeding: An employer conducted a disciplinary enquiry into the employee’s conduct.
predicates.criminal_acquittal: A criminal court acquitted the employee of the alleged offence.
predicates.acquittal_based_on_benefit_of_doubt: The criminal court acquitted the employee because the prosecution did not establish guilt to the required criminal standard.
predicates.prosecution_witnesses_turned_hostile: One or more prosecution witnesses withdrew or resiled from their earlier statements during the criminal trial.

issues.definition: A criminal acquittal based on benefit of doubt or hostile witnesses does not prevent an employer from pursuing disciplinary action in a separate enquiry.

issues.legal_issue: Reinstatement is not warranted where the disciplinary record provides sufficient grounds to conclude that the employee’s connection with the incident would undermine public confidence in the police force.
material_facts: The employee had been acquitted of murder, but the disciplinary record included evidence of prior hostility, a death threat, and the employee’s and his tractor’s proximity to the place and time associated with the death.

The Supreme Court considered that this material could support the State’s concern about the effect of the employee’s continued service on the police force’s credibility, even if it would not sustain a criminal conviction for murder.
The High Court had directed reinstatement without back wages.
issues.conclusion: The Court set aside the direction for reinstatement. Under Article 142 of the Constitution, it directed that cessation from service be treated as occurring when the employee completed the minimum qualifying service, upheld the denial of back wages, and directed computation and release of retiral dues on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principles governing disciplinary proof and judicial review, and exercised its jurisdiction under Article 142 of the Constitution to shape the final relief. It relied on the distinction between criminal guilt and the broader question whether an employee’s continued service would impair public administration and confidence in the police.

predicates.appeal_against_reinstatement: An appeal challenges a court order directing that an employee be reinstated in service.
predicates.disciplinary_record_supports_public_conf: The disciplinary record contains material supporting the employer’s concern that the employee’s continued service could undermine public confidence in the relevant institution.
predicates.criminal_acquittal_does_not_resolve_serv: The employee’s criminal acquittal does not determine whether the employee is suitable to continue in the relevant service.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges reinstatement and the disciplinary record supports a concern about public confidence that the criminal acquittal does not resolve, the reinstatement direction may be set aside.
